title: Design a Distributed Message Queue (Kafka-like)
prompt: Design a distributed, durable, high-throughput message queue / streaming platform like Apache Kafka. Producers publish messages to topics; consumers read them, possibly in groups for parallelism. Cover partitioning, ordering guarantees, consumer groups and offset management, replication and durability, delivery semantics (at-least-once / at-most-once / exactly-once), and retention. Assume very high throughput and strong durability requirements.
blurb: The append-only partitioned log — ordering vs parallelism, consumer-group rebalancing, replication with ISR, and honest delivery semantics.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (publish, subscribe, topics/partitions, consumer groups, retention, replay) from non-functional (throughput, durability, ordering, delivery guarantees, latency).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about throughput, message size, ordering scope, delivery-semantics requirement, retention duration, replay, multi-DC.

rubric.label: Back-of-envelope estimations
rubric.description: Messages/s and MB/s ingest, storage per retention window, partition count, replication bandwidth.

rubric.label: Partitioned append-only log design
rubric.description: Topic → partitions, each an ordered append-only log on disk with offsets; partitioning key; sequential IO / page cache for throughput. Central staff signal.

rubric.label: Ordering guarantees
rubric.description: Per-partition total order vs no global order; partition key choice; ordering vs parallelism tradeoff; effect of producer retries on order.

rubric.label: Consumer groups & offset management
rubric.description: Group coordinator, partition assignment, rebalancing, committed offsets, at-least-once via commit-after-process, one consumer per partition per group. Central staff signal.

rubric.label: Replication & durability
rubric.description: Leader/follower per partition, ISR, acks levels, high-water-mark, leader election, no data loss on broker failure.

rubric.label: Delivery semantics
rubric.description: At-most-once vs at-least-once vs exactly-once; idempotent producer (sequence numbers), transactions, and consumer-side idempotency/dedup.

rubric.label: API design
rubric.description: produce (with acks/keys), fetch (offset-based), commit offset, subscribe/assign; admin (create topic).

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Producers → brokers (partition leaders) → replicated logs → consumers pulling by offset; coordinator role.

rubric.label: Retention, compaction & scaling
rubric.description: Time/size retention, log compaction, segment files, adding partitions/brokers, rebalancing data, tiered storage.

rubric.label: Bottlenecks
rubric.description: Hot partitions, rebalance storms, replication lag, consumer lag, disk IO, slow consumers.

rubric.label: Observability & reliability
rubric.description: Consumer lag, ISR shrink/under-replicated partitions, throughput, end-to-end latency, poison-message/DLQ handling.

functional_requirements: Topics are split into partitions for parallelism
Consumers subscribe, individually or in consumer groups for scale-out
Durable retention with replay from any offset within the window
Retention by time/size; optional log compaction
nonfunctional_requirements: Very high throughput (millions of messages/s, GB/s)
Durable — no acknowledged message lost on broker failure
Horizontal scalability of producers, consumers, and storage
Configurable delivery semantics up to exactly-once
clarifying_questions: Target throughput (messages/s and MB/s) and typical message size?
What ordering scope do consumers need — per-key, per-partition, or none?
Which delivery guarantee is required — at-most, at-least, or exactly-once?
Retention: how long must messages be replayable, and do we need compaction?
Do consumers pull or do we push to them?
qualifying_questions: Are producers okay trading latency (acks=all) for durability?
How many consumer groups and how sensitive to rebalance pauses?
Is tiered/cheap storage for old segments acceptable?

estimations.traffic: 1M messages/s × 1KB avg = ~1GB/s ingest. With replication factor 3, ~3GB/s of write + replication IO across the cluster.
estimations.storage: 1GB/s × 86400s ≈ ~86TB/day of raw log per replica; ×RF and ×retention days → petabytes; drives partition count and broker/disk sizing; old segments tiered to object storage.
estimations.partitions: Parallelism is bounded by partition count: to let a group of C consumers run in parallel you need ≥ C partitions; choose partitions for peak parallelism + headroom (repartitioning is disruptive).
estimations.replication: acks=all waits for the in-sync replica set; replication traffic ≈ (RF-1) × ingest.

core_components: Partitioned append-only commit log on disk (segment files + index)
data_model: topic → N partitions; each partition = ordered append-only log of records, each with a monotonically increasing offset
segment files per partition (active + rolled), with a sparse offset→position index
consumer_offsets(group_id, topic, partition, committed_offset) — durable, itself a compacted log
high_water_mark per partition = highest offset replicated to all ISR (consumer-visible boundary)
api_design: Produce: send(topic, key, value, acks=[0|1|all]) → partition chosen by hash(key); returns (partition, offset)
Fetch: poll(topic, partition, from_offset, max_bytes) → records[] (consumer pulls)
Subscribe(group, topics) → coordinator assigns partitions;  Assign(topic, partition) for manual
reference.high_level_design: A topic is divided into PARTITIONS; each partition is an ORDERED, APPEND-ONLY commit log persisted as segment files, and every record gets a monotonically increasing OFFSET. Throughput comes from sequential disk IO, OS page cache, zero-copy transfer, and producer batching/compression — not random writes. Each partition has one LEADER broker and RF-1 followers; producers write to the leader, which appends and replicates to followers. The IN-SYNC REPLICA (ISR) set tracks followers caught up to the leader; with acks=all a produce is acknowledged only once all ISR have it, and the HIGH-WATER-MARK (max offset present on all ISR) is the boundary consumers may read — guaranteeing durability and that consumers never read un-replicated data. On leader failure a controller elects a new leader from the ISR, so no acknowledged data is lost. Consumers PULL by offset (cheap replay, natural backpressure). A CONSUMER GROUP shares a topic's partitions: the group coordinator assigns each partition to exactly one consumer in the group, giving per-partition ordering with cross-partition parallelism; when members join/leave, a REBALANCE reassigns partitions. Consumers commit offsets (durably, to an offsets topic); at-least-once = commit AFTER processing (a crash re-delivers), at-most-once = commit before. Exactly-once uses an idempotent producer (per-partition sequence numbers dedup producer retries) plus transactions (atomic write + offset commit), with consumer-side idempotency for true end-to-end EOS. Retention is by time/size with old segments deleted or tiered; log compaction keeps the latest value per key for changelog topics.

deep_dives.probe: Why is a partition a single append-only log on disk instead of a database table, and how does that get you millions of messages a second? Talk me through sequential IO, page cache, zero-copy, batching, and how offsets and segment index files let a consumer seek.

A consumer needs all events for a given user in order but you also want parallelism. How do partitions give you that, what do you pick as the partition key, and what breaks ordering — including what a producer retry can do to order and how the idempotent producer fixes it?

Explain consumer groups: who assigns partitions, what exactly happens during a rebalance, and why can't two consumers in the same group read the same partition? A consumer processes a batch then crashes before committing — what does the next consumer see, and is that at-least-once or exactly-once?

Walk through acks=0/1/all and ISR. A broker leading a partition dies right after acking a write with acks=all — is the data safe, and how is the new leader chosen? What's the high-water-mark and why can't consumers read past it? When can you still lose data (unclean leader election)?

Define at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once precisely in this system. How does the idempotent producer dedup retries, how do transactions make the write-plus-offset-commit atomic, and why do you still need consumer-side idempotency for real end-to-end exactly-once?

A common use of this queue is ingesting database changes. If a producer is a CDC/Debezium connector streaming a DB's changelog into a topic, how do you preserve per-row ordering, handle the connector restarting (duplicates), and use log compaction to keep the latest state per key?

Brokers rely heavily on the OS page cache for hot tail reads; a fleet of consumers doing historical replay evicts the hot pages and thrashes disk — a cache stampede at the storage layer. How do you protect tail-read latency — read throttling/quotas, tiered storage for old segments, isolating replay consumers?

followup_bank.question: Why an append-only log per partition, and how do sequential IO + page cache + zero-copy + batching get you GB/s? How do segment index files enable offset seeks?
What's your partition key, and how can a producer retry reorder messages within a partition — how does the idempotent producer prevent it?
Who coordinates assignment, what happens during a rebalance, and after a crash-before-commit is redelivery at-least-once or exactly-once?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions replication or acks or isr
followup_bank.question: Explain acks=all + ISR + high-water-mark, how a new leader is elected on failure, and when unclean leader election can still lose data.
How does the idempotent producer dedup retries, how do transactions atomically commit write+offset, and why is consumer-side idempotency still required end-to-end?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions cdc or debezium or database
followup_bank.question: If the producer is a CDC/Debezium connector, how do you preserve per-row ordering and dedup on connector restart, and how does log compaction keep latest-per-key?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions cache or page cache or replay
followup_bank.question: How do you stop replay/backfill consumers from evicting hot tail pages and thrashing disk — quotas, tiered storage, consumer isolation?

scaling: Add partitions for more parallelism (bounded by consumer count); plan capacity since repartitioning is disruptive
Add brokers and rebalance partition replicas across them
Tiered storage: offload cold segments to object storage, keep hot tail on local disk
Producer batching + compression to raise effective throughput
Isolate heavy replay consumers with quotas
bottlenecks: Hot partition from a skewed key (one key dominating)
Rebalance storms pausing consumption on membership churn
Replication lag shrinking ISR and threatening durability/availability
Disk IO and page-cache thrash from historical replay
tradeoffs: More partitions (parallelism, replay) vs fewer (less overhead, faster rebalance, more ordering scope)
acks=all (durable, higher latency) vs acks=1/0 (fast, risk loss)
At-least-once (simple, duplicates) vs exactly-once (no dupes, transaction overhead/latency)
Long retention/replay (flexible, costly storage) vs short
Push (low latency, hard backpressure) vs pull (backpressure-friendly, poll latency) — pull chosen
Ordering (single partition per key, limits parallelism) vs throughput
alternative_solutions: Traditional broker with per-message ack + queue (RabbitMQ-style) — richer routing, weaker replay/throughput
Pulsar-style separation of compute (brokers) and storage (bookies) for independent scaling
Cloud log services (Kinesis/PubSub) — managed, less control
KRaft/Raft-based metadata instead of an external coordinator like ZooKeeper
observability: Consumer lag per group/partition (the key health metric)
Under-replicated / offline partitions and ISR shrink alerts
End-to-end produce→consume latency and broker throughput
Poison-message handling / dead-letter queue and reprocessing
Disk usage vs retention, tiered-storage offload rate
security: AuthN (mTLS/SASL) and per-topic ACLs for produce/consume
Encryption in transit; at-rest encryption of segments
Quotas to prevent a noisy tenant starving others
Audit of admin ops (topic create/ACL change)
reference.reference_answer: A staff-level answer models a topic as PARTITIONS, each an ordered append-only commit log with monotonic offsets, and explains that throughput comes from sequential IO, page cache, zero-copy, and batching. Each partition has a leader + followers with an ISR; acks=all + high-water-mark give durability (no acknowledged data lost, consumers never read un-replicated records), and a controller elects a new leader from the ISR on failure — with an honest note on unclean leader election. Ordering is per-partition via the partition key, explicitly traded against parallelism, and the candidate knows a producer retry can reorder and that the idempotent producer (sequence numbers) fixes it. Consumer groups assign each partition to one member via a coordinator, rebalance on membership change, and commit offsets durably; commit-after-process = at-least-once, and true exactly-once needs the idempotent producer + transactions (atomic write+offset commit) plus consumer-side idempotency. They cover retention/compaction/tiered storage, treat consumer lag and under-replicated partitions as the core health signals, and name hot partitions, rebalance storms, replication lag, and page-cache thrash from replay as the main bottlenecks with mitigations. Bonus: CDC-connector-as-producer ordering/restart handling and pull-based backpressure.

interviewer_notes: Staff bar: precise reasoning about the log abstraction, ordering-vs-parallelism, replication/ISR durability, and honest delivery semantics — not buzzwords. Make them explain WHY a partition is an append-only log and how that yields GB/s (sequential IO, page cache, zero-copy, batching). Force precision on delivery semantics: many candidates claim 'exactly-once' loosely — push until they separate idempotent producer, transactions, and consumer-side idempotency, and admit at-least-once + idempotent consumer is the common real answer. Drive the consumer-group deep-dive (assignment, rebalance, crash-before-commit) and replication (acks/ISR/HWM/leader election, unclean election data loss). This is a queue, so use the CDC probe as 'the producer IS a Debezium connector — preserve ordering and dedup on restart', and the cache probe as page-cache thrash from replay consumers. Watch for red flags: global ordering claims, push-based with no backpressure story, or ignoring rebalance/lag. Reserve time for retention/compaction/tiered storage and observability (lag, under-replicated partitions).
